questions.stem: Find all values of $p$ such that the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sqrt{\frac{k^3 + 3k}{k^p + 2}}$ converges.
questions.solution:
$$
\sqrt{\frac{k^3 + 3k}{k^p + 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + 3/k^2}{1 + 2/k^p}} \cdot \frac{k^{3/2}}{k^{p/2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + 3/k^2}{1 + 2/k^p}} \cdot \frac{1}{k^{\frac{p-3}{2}}}
$$

Hence

$$
\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{\sqrt{\frac{k^3+3k}{k^p+2}}}{1/k^{\frac{p-3}{2}}} = 1
$$

Since $\sum \frac{1}{k^{\frac{p-3}{2}}}$ converges only if $\frac{p-3}{2} > 1$, that is $p > 5$, the series converges only if $p > 5$.

questions.stem: Which of the statements below is true for the series $\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^{-m}}{\sin(m) + 2}$?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparison test is not applicable.

questions.solution:
$2 + \sin m \ge 1$. Therefore

$$
0 \le \frac{3^{-m}}{2 + \sin(m)} \le 3^{-m}
$$

Since $\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} 3^{-m}$ converges, so does the series.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

$$
I.\ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2k+1}; \quad II.\ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}+1}; \quad III.\ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^2+1}
$$
questions.solution:
I. Diverges by comparison with $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}$:

$$
\frac{1}{2k+1} \ge \frac{1}{4k}, \qquad \sum \frac{1}{2k+1} \ge \sum \frac{1}{4k}
$$

II. Converges by the alternating series test.

III. $k^2 + 1 \ge k^2$, so $\frac{1}{k^2+1} \le \frac{1}{k^2}$. $\sum \frac{1}{k^2+1}$ converges by comparison with $\sum \frac{1}{k^2}$.

questions.stem: Consider $S = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{m-1}\frac{1}{m^4}$ and its partial sum $S_n = \sum_{m=1}^{n}(-1)^{m-1}\frac{1}{m^4}$. According to the alternating series estimation theorem, what is the smallest $n$ such that $|S - S_n| \le 16 \times 10^{-8}$?
questions.solution:
By the alternating series estimation theorem,

$$
|S - S_n| \le b_{n+1} = \frac{1}{(n+1)^4} \le 16 \times 10^{-8}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{(n+1)^4} \le \frac{2^4}{10^8}, \qquad \frac{1}{n+1} \le \frac{2}{10^2}
$$

So $n + 1 \ge \frac{100}{2} = 50$, and $n \ge 49$.

questions.stem:
Which of the statements is true about the following series?

$$
I.\ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\cos(n); \quad II.\ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{1}{\ln(n+1)}; \quad III.\ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{\sqrt{n}+1}{n}.
$$

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only II and III are convergent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only I and II are convergent

questions.solution:
I. $\lim_{n\to\infty}\cos n$ does not exist, so the terms do not tend to $0$ and I diverges.

II. Alternating series; converges.

III. Also alternating; converges.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false?

choices.label: B
choices.text: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} r^n$ diverges for all $r$ such that $|r| \ge 1$.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ is convergent, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n$ is also convergent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ is divergent, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n$ is also divergent.

questions.solution:
A. True; integral test.

B. True; geometric series.

C. False.

D. True; comparison test.

E. True; ratio test.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

$$
S_1 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^n}{4^n + 5^n}, \quad S_2 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n^2}{n^3 + 5n}, \quad S_3 = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{\ln n}{n},
$$
questions.solution:
$S_1$:

$$
\frac{3^n}{4^n + 5^n} = \frac{3^n}{5^n} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + (4/5)^n} \approx \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^n
$$

Since $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{3^n}{5^n}$ converges, so does $S_1$.

$S_2$:

$$
\frac{n^2}{n^3 + 5n} = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + 5/n^2}
$$

Since $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges, so does $S_2$.

$S_3$: $\frac{\ln n}{n} \ge \frac{1}{n}$ for $n \ge 3$, so $S_3$ diverges too.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

$$
S_1 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{n!}{10^n}, \quad S_2 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{10^n}{(n+1)^n}, \quad S_3 = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n^8\, 2^{-n},
$$
questions.solution:
$S_1$: $a_n = \frac{n!}{10^n}$.

$$
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)!}{10^{n+1}} \times \frac{10^n}{n!} = \frac{n+1}{10} \to \infty
$$

so $S_1$ diverges.

$S_2$: $a_n = \left(\frac{10}{n+1}\right)^n$, and $|a_n|^{1/n} = \frac{10}{n+1} \to 0$, so $S_2$ converges.

$S_3$: $a_n = n^8 2^{-n}$.

$$
\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)^8}{2^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{2^n}{n^8} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^8 \to \frac{1}{2}
$$

so $S_3$ converges.

questions.stem: Find the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-1)^n}{n\, 3^n}$.
questions.solution:
$a_n = \frac{(x-1)^n}{n\,3^n}$, $x \ne 1$.

$$
\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{|x-1|^{n+1}}{(n+1) \cdot 3^{n+1}} \times \frac{n\,3^n}{|x-1|^n} = \frac{|x-1|}{3} \cdot \frac{n}{n+1} \to \frac{|x-1|}{3} < 1
$$

$|x - 1| < 3$, so $-3 < x - 1 < 3$ and $-2 < x < 4$.

Endpoints: at $x = 4$, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ diverges. At $x = -2$, $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges.

The interval is $[-2, 4)$.

questions.stem:
Let $b_n > 0$ and $a_n$ be such that

$$
a_{n+1} = (-1)^{n+1}\left(\frac{n+1}{2n+7}\right)a_n \text{ for } n \ge 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|a_n|}{b_n} = 2.
$$

We can say that the following are true:

choices.label: A
choices.text: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ converges absolutely and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n$ converges

choices.label: B
choices.text: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ converges conditionally and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n$ converges

choices.label: D
choices.text: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ converges absolutely and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n$ diverges

questions.solution:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n+1}{2n+7} = \frac{1}{2}
$$

So $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely.

Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_n}{b_n}\right| = 2$ and $\sum |a_n|$ converges, $\sum |b_n|$ converges, but $b_n > 0$, so $\sum b_n$ converges.
